excerpt: Changing your domain does not have to break your site. Here is how to change the domain name of a WordPress site safely, step by step.

faqs.a: It can cause a short dip, but a proper move with page to page 301 redirects and a change of address in Search Console protects most of your rankings. The damage comes from broken redirects or letting the old domain expire, not from the change itself.
faqs.q: Will changing my domain name hurt my Google rankings?

faqs.a: No. You keep the same site, the same content, and the same design. You are only changing the address it lives at, then updating the stored links and redirecting the old address to the new one.
faqs.q: Do I need to rebuild my WordPress site to change the domain?

faqs.a: The WordPress part can be done in an hour or two on a simple site. DNS changes can take a few hours to spread, and Google can take a few weeks to fully process the move. Plan the switch for a quiet period if you can.
faqs.q: How long does a domain change take?

faqs.a: Yes, for at least a year. The old domain is what makes your redirects work. If you let it expire, anyone using an old link gets an error page, and you lose the ranking value those links carried.
faqs.q: Should I keep paying for my old domain?

intro:
A business outgrows its name. You rebrand, you move to a shorter address, or the name you started with just does not fit anymore. Whatever the reason, changing your domain name is a normal part of growing a business, and WordPress makes it doable.

The risk is not the change itself. It is doing it halfway. If your old address keeps pointing nowhere, or your site still loads half its images from the old domain, visitors get confused and Google loses track of your pages. Done in the right order, though, a domain change is a clean move, not a mess.

This guide walks you through the whole job in plain terms: what to prepare, how to make the switch inside WordPress, and how to check that everything still works afterwards. You do not need to be a developer to follow it, but if you have one, hand them this checklist and the job gets much simpler.
keyword: how to change the domain name of a wordpress site
meta: Learn how to change the domain name of a WordPress site without losing traffic, links, or rankings. A safe, step by step guide for business owners.

body: Start with a full backup of your site, files and database together. Most good hosting panels offer a one click backup, and backup plugins can do the same. Save a copy somewhere safe, not just on the same server.

This backup is your safety net. If anything goes wrong during the move, you can restore the site exactly as it was and try again. Never skip this step because the change looks simple. Domain changes touch every link on your site, so a small mistake can spread quickly.

While you are at it, note down your current setup: your hosting login, your domain registrar login, and where your email is hosted. Changing a domain can affect email too, so you want those details handy before you start.
sections.heading: Before You Touch Anything: Make a Backup

body: Buy or register your new domain first, before changing anything in WordPress. Then point it at your hosting account. Your host will give you nameservers or a DNS record to add at your registrar, and it can take a few hours for that change to spread across the internet.

Wait until the new domain actually loads your hosting account before moving on. You can test this by visiting the new address in a browser. If it shows a hosting placeholder page, the pointing is working and you are ready for the next step.

If your email uses your domain, check with your host or email provider before changing DNS records. A careless DNS change can stop your email working, and that is a problem you want to avoid on moving day.
sections.heading: Register the New Domain and Point It at Your Hosting

body: In your WordPress dashboard, go to Settings, then General. You will see two fields: WordPress Address and Site Address. Change both to your new domain, including the correct https part, and save.

You will be logged out right after saving, and that is normal. Log back in using the new domain. If you cannot log in, or the site looks broken, do not panic. Your host can usually fix the address directly in the database, and this is a common support request.

For most simple sites, this one change updates the main address. But older posts, images, and links inside your content may still point to the old domain. That is why the next steps matter just as much as this one.
sections.heading: Update the Address Inside WordPress

body: Your database stores the old domain in many places: inside post content, image addresses, menus, and widgets. A search and replace tool updates all of them at once. Plugins built for this job handle the database safely, including the serialized data WordPress uses.

Run the replacement carefully, old domain to new domain, and check the results before you call it done. A good tool shows you how many rows changed. If the count looks wildly wrong, stop and restore your backup rather than pushing ahead.
Do not try to edit the database by hand unless you know exactly what you are doing. One wrong edit in the wrong table can take the whole site down, while a proper tool does the same job in minutes.
sections.heading: Update Every Old Link With Search and Replace

body: This is the step that protects your traffic. Set up a permanent redirect, called a 301 redirect, from every page on the old domain to the matching page on the new domain. Anyone who clicks an old link, and Google itself, will land on the right new page automatically.

Your host can often set this up for you, or a redirection plugin can handle it inside WordPress. The key point is that it must be page to page, not everything to the homepage. Sending all old pages to your homepage loses visitors and confuses search engines.

Keep the old domain registered and the redirect running for at least a year, ideally longer. Old links live on in bookmarks, social posts, and other websites for a long time, and the redirect is what keeps them working.
sections.heading: Redirect the Old Domain to the New One

body: Your new domain needs its own security certificate so it loads over https with the padlock showing. Most hosts issue this free and automatically once the domain points at them, but check it. A missing certificate gives visitors a scary warning instead of your site.

Now go through the site like a customer would. Open the homepage, a few inner pages, and your contact form. Click images and links. Check that your logo, menus, and forms all load, and that nothing still points to the old domain.

Also update the places that point to your site: your Google Business Profile, social media bios, email signature, and any business listings. These are easy to forget, and they are often where new customers first find you.
sections.heading: Fix Your Security Certificate and Check the Site

body: If you use Google Search Console, add the new domain as a property and use the change of address tool. This tells Google directly that your site has moved, which helps it transfer your rankings to the new address faster.

Then keep an eye on things for a few weeks. Watch Search Console for errors, check that your key pages are being indexed under the new domain, and look at your traffic. A small dip right after a move is normal, but it should recover as Google processes the redirects.

If traffic stays down after a few weeks, check the basics first: are the redirects still working, is the new site indexed, and did any pages get missed in the search and replace? Most post-move problems trace back to one of those three.
